rv.q: Longhurst's revival is correspondingly both a Middle England sitcom and a psychedelic fever dream.
It’s so cheering to see the West End can still take risks, and even more encouraging to know that Smith and co will be taking the play out of London, albeit briefly, after the run finishes.
When it works, it is unnerving.
This revival of Woman in Mind is gripping and deeply resonant.
When the derangement climaxes, Smith cowering under a bench, drenched to the skin, its power comes despite the production rather than because of it.
Smith can't do much to disguise the fact that this is frivolous fare, unlikely to become a set text for students of either contemporary theatre or psychology.
Four decades on from its premiere, the play sometimes still startles, but in the end it simply doesn’t cut it.
It’s a lovely, naturalistic performance, but it exposes the artificiality of the play.
Always a performer to bring every emotion to a role, Smith shows a gradual mental disintergration, becoming increasingly fractious as she grapples with what is real and what is fantasy.
Though Susan may lose her grip on reality, this Woman In Mind never risks losing its grip on the audience, ensuring it will linger in my mind long after the safety curtain falls.

His dialogue — snappy and laden with pithy meaning even in the intentionally stylised moments — reminds us of the fragility of mental stability and the constant need for compassion and understanding in our daily interactions.
